threads.question:
Dear Officer,
In a scenario where the sponsor resides in Quebec for the last three years; however the sponsor ONLY meets the provincial financial requirements for one year preceding the application date.
Considering the following:
Sponsors living inQuebec
The goverment of Quebec is responsible for determining whether or not sponsors lrving in the province have the
financial ability to sponsor family members and also the length of their undertaking
It the federal eligibility requirements are met, the Case Processing Centre in Mississauga (CPC-M) will send the sponsor a lelter with instructions to downioad the MIDI undertaking kit, then to complete and submit it to the MiIDi with a

Question 1: Once a sponsor provides the necessary proof, financial documents for one year preceding the application date, according to the provincial requirements, should financial documents for one year only (as per government of Quebec requirements) be sufficient to pass the completeness check at the federal level?

Thank you in advance.
Sincerely,
and Citizenship Caneda
Blank Page
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Dear Sir/ Madam,
Thank you for your inquiry
The Canada-Quebec Accord gives Quebec responsibility for setting its own criteria for family class sponsorship and administering undertakings. The federal government maintains responsibility for program eligibility requirements and for matters related to admissibility and enforcement. Quebec is responsible for determining the financial criteria for the sponsorship of foreign nationals intending to live in Quebec, and administering sponsorship undertakings and determining their duration. As of result of this Accord, sponsors who live in the province of Quebec do not have to submit the form Financial Evaluation for Parents and Grandparents Sponsorship (IMM 5768).
Please note that the form Application to Sponsor, Sponsorship Agreement and Undertaking (IMM 1344) must be included in your submission to sponsor. On the form itself and in the instructions guide, questions not to be answer by sponsors who live in the province of Quebec are indicated.

Their study permit expires in the spring, commensurate with the expiry of their passport. They have been unable to secure a passport renewal from within Canada, and are required to return to their country of citizenship in order to apply for and receive the new passport. In short, they required a National ID card to apply for a passport renewal, however they have resided outside their country of citizenship since they were a minor and did not have a National ID card. They made a trip to their home country over the winter holiday break to apply for their National ID, but did not have it in time to also apply for a passport renewal. Their consular office in Canada will not be able to facilitate the issuance of a new passport for at least six months, and have advised the student to return home to their country of citizenship, where they will be able to apply for and receive a new passport in ~2 weeks.

and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
school term ends in May, at which point they plan to apply for their new passport, as well as their new study permit to return to their schooling in September.
The student's current plan is to apply for an in-land study permit extension just before their study permit expires, to enter implied status and allow them to remain in Canada legally to finish out the school term. After the term in over, they will return to their country of citizenship, procure their new passport, and apply for a new study permit to return for the subsequent 2 years remaining in their program.
Are there any alternatives to this scenario to allow the student to remain in Canada, besides resorting to implied status? Can you comment on the feasibility of this plan?
Many thanks for your feedback,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
of term-REP-2017-0163
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry of January 30th regarding alternative options for a student to finish their school year while their study permit and passport expire before the end of the semester.
Subject to section 189 of the IRPR, a foreign national who has made an application under subsection 217(1) is authorized to study without a study permit until a decision is made on the application if they have remained in Canada since the expiry of their study permit and continue to comply with the conditions, other than the expiry date, set out on the expired study permit.
To benefit from implied status, the applicant must apply before the expiration of their study permit and provide all required documents along with their application, as indicated in the application guide. Please note that if their application is refused or returned due to incompletion, the applicant will no longer benefit from their implied status and will be considered out of status in Canada.

threads.subject: Unaccompanied minor children studying in Canada -REP-2017-0277-
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I am seeking some guidance as to whether: (i) unaccompanied minor children require study permits to study in Canada if the duration is less than six months or if can they apply for visitor admission and study in Canada at the secondary level based on the fact that they hold valid visitor status? and (ii) whether unaccompanied minor children who enter Canada on visitor records for a period of six months to enroll in a course of studies of less than six months i.e. one term of high school, but who then subsequently decide to continue their studies in Canada, can apply to amend and extend their status from visitor to student inside Canada or if all they need to do to continue studying inside Canada is to extend their visitor status based on the fact that they are already in Canada, studying at the secondary level and neither parent is physically in Canada? My understanding is that a child who is already inside Canada and unaccompanied may not require a study permit
- [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/minors-documents.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/minors-documents.asp) We have seen situations where unaccompanied minor students in Canada who hold visitor records have applied to amend and extend their status from visitor to student inside Canada and have been advised by CPC Vegreville that they do not
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
qualify to apply for their study permit inside Canada and need to apply outside Canada. In other identical scenarios, the study permit has issued.
If there is a Custodian in Canada for a child who is aged between 17 and 19, but the child upon arriving in Canada/after spending part of the authorized duration in Canada and/or turning 18 advises the Custodian that s/he will be seeking his or her own accommodation independently and may or may not continue to attend school in Canada, aside from the child's parents, to whom should the Custodian report this information as that Custodian is no longer in a situation where s/he can meet his or her obligations as set out in the Custodianship Declaration?
Many thanks in advance for your guidance.
Kind regards,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your enquiry from February 27, 2017 regarding study permits for unaccompanied minors.
In general, if applying from outside Canada with the intent to study once in Canada, the minor is required to apply for a study permit before entering Canada.
As per [A30(2)] minor children already in Canada are authorized to study without a study permit at the secondary level if neither parent is physically in Canada.
The client can continue studying in secondary school without a permit until they reach the age of majority in the province so long as they continue holding valid visitor status; once they reach the age of majority, they would be required to hold a valid study permit to continue their studies.
The Custodianship Declaration notes that the custodian is required to meet their obligations until the minor student reaches the age of majority. If circumstances change, they can be communicated to IRCC through the IRCC Web Form. Note that as per IRPR 220.1(1)(b), the holder of a study permit should actively pursue their course or program of study in order to maintain the validity of the permit.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Traveling to Canada as Visitor while IEC work permit application in process -
threads.question:
Good morning,
If an individual residing outside of Canada submits an application for a Working Holiday work permit under the International Experience Class program, are there any rules or regulations that prevent that individual from travelling to Canada as a visitor while the work permit application is in process at an overseas visa office?
Many thanks in advance for your assistance.
Best regards,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
REP-2017-0177
Dear Ms.
Question:
If an individual residing outside of Canada submits an application for a Working Holiday work permit under the International Experience Class program, are there any rules or regulations that prevent that individual from travelling to Canada as a visitor while the work permit application is in process at an overseas visa office?
Response:
There are no rules or regulations that prevent an individual from travelling to Canada as a visitor while they have a work permit application in process. However, they must meet all the requirements to enter Canada as a visitor depending on their country of nationality (visa, eTA). In addition, foreign nationals who seek to enter Canada temporarily must satisfy an officer that they:
•intend to return to their home country and will not try to remain in Canada;
- have enough money to cover travel costs and support themselves while in Canada;
- do not intend to work or study in Canada unless they have a permit to do so;
- do not have a criminal record or are not a security risk; and are in good health (or have completed a medical examination, if required).
The applicant must keep in mind that the border services officer may question the true purpose of their visit to Canada given that they have a work permit application in process.
In the event that the applicant is in Canada as a visitor and the application under International Experience Canada (IEC) is refused, the applicant will not be authorized to work in Canada and will have to comply with any conditions imposed at the port of entry (POE).
If the application under lEC is approved, the applicant will need to present their letter of introduction at a POE, which means they will have to exit Canada if they entered Canada as visitor. They'll need this letter of introduction to receive a work permit under International Experience Canada when they enter Canada and show it to a border services officer at the port of entry (airport, land border, etc.). The letter does not guarantee entry into Canada or guarantee a work permit.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
*and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada

threads.subject: Supervisa "extension" REP-2017-0419-
threads.question:
Hello,
If a visa exempt US citizen were to obtain a 2 year supervisa, how would they “extend” it for another 2 year supervisa? Would they have to submit a new TRV application online from “outside Canada"? Or, could they apply online to extend from within Canada before the supervisa expires and benefit from implied status?
Thank you very much,
and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good day,
Foreign nationals who do not require a temporary resident visa to enter Canada who wish to benefit from the super visa program, must complete and submit the requested documents as outlined on our website at the following link: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/visit/supervisa-how.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/visit/supervisa-how.asp). If the application is approved they will be provided with a letter of introduction that can be presented at the port of entry where a Border Services Officer may approve a visit to Canada for up to two years. Super visa clients in Canada who have valid temporary status may apply to extend their status from within Canada. As with all temporary residents seeking extension, super visa clients are assessed as regular visitors. The length of the extension is at the discretion of the processing officer. Detailed application instructions can be found here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/visitor.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/visitor.asp).

threads.answer:
[mailto: ] '
Dear Mr.
Thank you for your email correspondence to Citizenship and Immigration Canada's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Your Question: How can an FSWC PR application be filed under IRPR 76(3) since the Express Entry System does not allow for this option under Canadian Immigration law.
Answer: It is not possible to submit an application for permanent residence under any of the immigration programs now managed through Express Entry without being invited to do so as a candidate in the Express Entry pool.
Therefore, only those candidates who meet the eligibility criteria for entry into the Express Entry pool and who receive an Invitation to Apply from IRCC are able to apply through the electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR).
Substituted evaluation for FSW cannot be used to overcome a prospective candidate's failure to meet minimum entry criteria in the creation of an Express Entry profile. An Express Entry profile is not an application. There is no provision for substituted evaluation in the Ministerial Instructions governing the submission of an expression of interest (i.e. Express Entry profile) to immigrate to Canada.
This means that substitution of evaluation under IPRP 76(3) may only be considered in limited circumstances by an officer for applications made under Express Entry (i.e. a change in circumstance after an applicant has been deemed to meet the minimum requirements of the program to which they have been invited to apply and the requirements of section 11.2 of IRPA).
We hope this information will assist you.

Citoyenneté Canada

threads.subject: To confirm that no new Offer of Employment is Required-REP-2017-0411
threads.question:
Hello,
Could you please confirm that under the following circumstance, there is no requirement to submit a new offer of employment online through an employer's portal?
Work Permit issued under the intra company transfer category Work to be performed in Canada is intermittent. The employee has not relocated to Canada. This was fully disclosed in the offer of employment and in work permit application Original home country was Chile. Employee was to remain on Chilean payroll, and not receive payment from
Canadian entity. This also was accurately disclosed in the Offer of Employment.
In January 2017, the employee was relocated from the employer's entity in Chile to the employer's entity in the US. Nothing about her role in Canada has changed. The required qualifying relationships between entities in Chile, US and Canada still exist The only variance from what was represented in the online offer of employment to the new circumstance is that instead of remaining on Chilean payroll, she has transferred to US payroll. Salary remains the equivalent amount as what was represented in the original Offer of Employment.
Since there has been no substantive change in the employee's role in Canada, the employee's eligibility to qualify under the category under which her work permit was issued, or other relevant terms of employment represented in the online Offer of Employment, I do not believe the employer would need to submit a new Offer of Employment to reflect the variance in currency of her salary. However, to ensure that the employer remains compliant with IRCC's requirements, please confirm that this understanding is correct.
Thank you very much in advance for your reply,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good day,
Response for sending. Please close item.
If the foreign transferer plans to now have the U.S. entity pay the wage of the intra-company transferee, this would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. A foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker, such as —employer, hours worked, wages paid, occupation or location.
Since there is no change in the job, the Canadian entity is still considered the primary employer.
As you know, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
Proactive notification of salary changes is not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages paid are what was stated in the offer of employment regardless of the source of the pay. Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the offer of employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Furthermore, if the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based wishes to ensure that the situation is very clear in case an inspection occurs, they may choose to submit a new offer of employment reflecting the new wage situation in the alternate compensation scheme' field of the Employer Portal AND have the worker obtain a new work permit based on the new offer of employment.
However, regardless of who is paying the wage, the primary employer will always be responsible for ensuring that the worker is paid what was offered in the Offer of Employment for which the work permit was issued.
and Cizenship Caneda
Regards,

REP-2017-0458-
Good day,
Question: Once an individual has been issued a Work Permit under an LMiA exemption, if there are any changes to the job (for example, job position, title, salary, benefits, etc.), is there a way to inform of these changes?
Answer:
In the case of an LMiA-exempt work permit, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer (the employer who submitted the Offer of Employment) by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
Employer conditions: Each work permit is issued based on the offer of employment provided. Once the work permit is issued the employer must meet the conditions in that offer until the end of the work permit. If the employer changes the offer – e.g. for example, job position, title, salary, benefits – then a new offer of employment and a new work permit is required. For each offer there can be only one work permit that triggers the conditions on the employer (and condition on foreign national listed on work permit). If the employment changes and the employer wishes to change the conditions that apply to themselves (employer) then a new offer and a new work permit is required. The old work permit would only apply to the original offer and in the information listed in that offer.
IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at time of inspection. The employer is required to retain all documents related to the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
More information can be found in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website-see the section "Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions:

From Pelletier.Sylvie ; Bernard.Paul

Hope all is well in Ottawa. I am writing in regards to the procedures when encountering a suspended/revoked rep while processing.

threads.answer:
Hi
Thanks for your questions on representatives.
As per the Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs) on "Use of Representatives", there is a section titled "Initial Screening" that advises IRCC staff to check the status of a representative noted on a the Use of a Representative IMM5476. IRCC staff are to check if that representative is a member of a Canadian provincial law society or is a member of the Immigration Consultant of Canada Regulatory Council (ICCRC).
Some authorized representatives submit high volumes of applications and are fairly well-known in many processing offices. Therefore, the following is found on the "Initial Screening" page:
It is not necessary to verify for each application from a given representative that they are a member in good standing, especially when the local office is familiar with the representative as an authorized member of one of the regulatory bodies. However, occasional verification is advisable.
Regarding the specific application you cited, we conducted some research and found that the IMM5476 for the first representative was added to GCMS in November 2015. At that time, that first representative was in good standing with the ICCRC, which means that whomever in IRCC entered that representative in GCMS did so correctly. Then, in October 2016, that first representative no longer held good standing due to administrative suspension. In March 2017, the HK VO sent a letter, 'Use of an Unauthorized Representative', to the address provided on the application. Later that same month a new representative was appointed, and this new representative is in good standing with a provincial law society.
Please be advised that the ICCRC sends to our office updates on the status of members, providing information as to when an ICCRC member has returned to his or her practice and is therefore once again in good standing, or when an ICCRC member is no longer in good standing, for whatever reason, Accordingly, our office then updates the members' status in GCMS.
We understand the vulnerabilities regarding whether you are speaking with the actual applicant, or whether it is the applicant's representative. Representatives are supposed to only use the Representative Portal, and not meant to use the My Application portal, and they should self-identify when corresponding with the Department.
Thank you,

Hello,
We are lawyers who represent a number of foreign airlines that operate in Canada. One of them, an carrier based in the USA, has retained us to clarify entry and work permit requirements for aircraft mechanics (Aircraft Maintenance Technicians in the US, equivalent to what is known as Aircraft Maintenance Engineers in Canada – both designations are granted by each country's federal government, in the US by the Federal Aviation Administration, in Canada by Transport Canada). I am writing to confirm my understanding and to ask questions about those requirements.
We have been asked about two situations, the first I think is relatively straightforward, the second perhaps less so.
Scenario #1 Our client, "USA Carrier", requires that maintenance be performed on one of its aircraft while it is in Canada and so flies up one or more of its mechanics from the US to perform the work.
It is my understanding that a work permit is required, but that this situation is LMIA exempt. That is, aircraft mechanics are not considered “crew” and therefore are not exempt from the requirement to obtain a work permit under R186(s) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The work permit processing fee ($155) and employer compliance fee ($230) apply. Further, it is my understanding that, while there has long been a work permit processing fee, the employer compliance fee was only instituted in February 2015.
However, we have been told that “filling out forms" and "paying certain fees" is not always required and/or has not been required in the past.
Questions:
1) Is my understanding correct? If not, how am I wrong? Understanding is correct. FN doesn't have to 'fill out
forms' at POE as WP application is verbal. However, ER has to fill out Offer in advance since Feb 2015.
2) Is the appropriate LMIA exemption code T11? (see here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp)) - I would say C13 or T23 (if the mechanic is an Engineer) but not T11 unless they have the specific Agreement.
3) Is exemption code C13 a possibility as well? Are there others? Yes, if the maintenance is required in order for
aircraft to be certified to leave the ground. If maintenance can wait for plane to return to foreign country then no.
4) What are the requirements for entry, in terms of documentation? Offer of Employment by the employer and
work permit by the employee.
5) With respect to the comment we heard from our client, is it the case that work permits were not required at some point in the last few years? We can't comment on past individual cases. Every final decision on who enters Canada and with what specific authorization is done by CBSA based on the information presented to them at the time of entry.
6) Alternatively or in addition, is it the case that some mechanics may not be (or have been) required to obtain a work permit by individual border service officers (for instance, depending on the airport)?
7) Is there anything that can be done to streamline entry and processing of such mechanics on a airline-wide basis or otherwise? I would suggest that they provide an ‘Offer of Employment' for a 12 month period indicating an ‘estimated time in Cda' in the Alternative Compensation Scheme area.
Scenario #2 Our client, “USA Carrier”, has been asked by a Canadian airline, “CAD Carrier”, to provide mechanics to assist in repairing CAD Carrier's aircraft because CAD Carrier lacks mechanics with expertise in the particular aircraft in question. CAD Carrier and USA Carrier are not related companies, but have a partnership or alliance with one another for certain purposes. As I understand it, as contemplated now, the support would be provided simply because the airlines are partners and the mechanics would only be paid their regular salaries by USA Carrier.
Questions:
1) May USA Carrier mechanics come to Canada on a temporary basis to perform repair work for CAD Carrier? - would be looking at T23 Professionals if the mechanic has an engineering degree or LMIA – CAD Carrier would to prove skills not available in Cda.
2) I assume a work permit would be required, but anticipate that the T11 exemption does not apply – would the C13 exemption be a possibility? Must we look to NAFTA rules?
2) If it is possible, please describe how and what requirements must be met or arrangements must be made.
Please let me know if anything above is unclear or you require further information. Thanks in advance.
Best regards,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Dear
Please note that where an employer believes that a foreign national is eligible for a LMIA exemption or a work permit exemption (e.g., business visitor), they can request an opinion from one of IRCC's International Mobility Worker Units (IMWU) if the foreign worker is from a visa-exempt country and is currently outside Canada. The opinion given by the Unit is considered by border services officers at the port of entry. Requests and supporting documentation must be submitted at least 30 days before the date of the worker plans to enter Canada. IMWUs contact information can be found here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/apply-who.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/apply-who.asp).
The IMWU service cannot be used if the foreign worker that an employer wants to hire is not from a visa-exempt country or is already in Canada. In such a case, it is the visa officer reviewing the work permit application who will determine if an LMIA exemption or a work permit exemption applies to the situation.
Scenario 1 Questions and Answers:
1) Is my understanding correct? If not, how am I wrong? Your understanding is correct. Foreign nationals do not have to 'fill out forms' at port of entry as the work permit application is verbal. However, the employer is required to fill out IRCC's 'Offer of Employment' in advance.
2) Is the appropriate LMIA exemption code T11? (see here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp)) - We would recommend C13 (Emergency repair personnel or repair personnel for out-of-warranty equipment) or T23NAFTA Professional (if the mechanic is an Engineer) but not T11 unless they have the specific agreement.
3) Is exemption code C13 a possibility as well? Are there others? Yes, if the maintenance is required in order for aircraft to be certified to leave the ground, as this may be emergency repair. If maintenance can wait for plane to return to foreign country then it would not be considered emergency repair.
4) What are the requirements for entry, in terms of documentation? By Regulation, the employer must provide the Offer of Employment using the Employer Portal prior to the foreign national's work permit application and the foreign worker must obtain a work permit.
5) With respect to the comment we heard from our client, is it the case that work permits were not required at some point in the last few years? We can't comment on past individual cases. Every final decision on who enters Canada and with what specific authorization is done by Canada Border Services Agency based on the information presented to them at the time of entry.
6) Alternatively or in addition, is it the case that some mechanics may not be (or have been) required to obtain a work permit by individual border service officers (for instance, depending on the airport)? Again, we cannot comment on past individual cases.
7) Is there anything that can be done to streamline entry and processing of such mechanics on a airline-wide basis or otherwise? We would suggest that they provide an 'Offer of Employment' for a 12 month period indicating an estimated time in Canada (e.g. employee will travel to Canada for 1 -2 days every week,...) in the Alternative Compensation Scheme area.
Scenario 2 Questions and Answers:
1) May USA Carrier mechanics come to Canada on a temporary basis to perform repair work for CAD Carrier? - We would recommend reviewing T23 NAFTA professionals if the mechanic has an engineering degree or obtaining a Labour Market Impact Assessment. The impetus would be on the Canadian carrier to prove skills not available in Canada.
2) I assume a work permit would be required, but anticipate that the T11 exemption does not apply – would the C13 exemption be a possibility? Must we look to NAFTA rules? C13 would only really apply if the maintenance was an emergency repair or on out-of-warranty equipment. Admission under this category would only be permitted for a short duration (i.e. less than 30 calendar days). For the mechanics to qualify under NAFTA, they would be required to have pre-arranged employment with the Canadian carrier, as well as be in possession of a Baccalaureate, Licenciatura Degree or state/provincial license.
3) If it is possible, please describe how and what requirements must be met or arrangements must be made. More on how to apply under NAFTA can be found here and information about applying under the C13 exemption can be found here.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Visitor Record holder applying for Inland SCLP & open work permit -REP-2017-0782
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
Could you please clarify whether a visa-exempt visitor record (VR) holder who has applied for PR and an open work permit under the inland spouse of common- law partner class will benefit from implied status once the VR expires?
Section 183(5) of the IRPR seems to contemplate this, but it is not clear whether the open work permit portion of the SCLP application will qualify as an application for “an extension of the period authorized for their stay”. Is this meant to cover only VR holders who are applying for another VR, or would an open work permit application be considered to satisfy this section as well?
- “Marginal note:Extension of period authorized for stay
(5) Subject to subsection (5.1), if a temporary resident has applied for an extension of the period authorized for their stay and a decision is not made on the application by the end of the period authorized for their stay, the period is extended until o (a) the day on which a decision is made, if the application is refused; or
(b) the end of the new period authorized for their stay, if the application is allowed."
Kindly,
Citoenneté Canada
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Thank you for your query to the Immigration Representatives mailbox. Please see the response to your question below.
QUESTION:
Section 183(5) of the IRPR seems to contemplate this, but it is not clear whether the open work permit portion of the SCLP application will qualify as an application for “an extension of the period authorized for their stay”. Is this meant to cover only VR holders who are applying for another VR, or would an open work permit application be considered to satisfy this section as well?
ANSWER:
A foreign national who submits the IMM 5710 Application to change conditions or extend my stay in Canada – Worker is in effect submitting two applications in one. The foreign national is applying under section 181 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) for an ‘extension of their status' and an application under section 200 for a work permit as they meet the requirement of who can apply from within Canada under R199.
If submitted prior to the expiry of their present status, this combined application has two effects:
1) should a decision not be made on the ‘application' under R181 prior to the expiration of their present status, the foreign national will be allowed to remain by operation of law (implied status) under R183(5), and
2) the application for work permit under R200 allows for the issuance of an open work permit on approval.
Kind regards,
The Immigration Representatives mailbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
On July 1, 2011, a moratorium on new applications was placed on the former Federal Entrepreneur program and in June 2014, applications still in the backlog of the federal Immigrant Investor Program and Entrepreneur Program were terminated. Unlike the former Entrepreneur program, Canada’s Start-Up Visa is the first of its kind in the world, as it links immigrant entrepreneurs with experienced private sector organizations that have expertise in working with start-ups. threads.subject: your reply about "substituted evaluation" in my opinion is not legally correct-
threads.question:
Immigration Representatives Thank you for your reply but unfortunately I am of the opinion that your explanation is not legally correct. Substituted evaluation exists in IRPR under Canadian Immigration law and regulations as a legal Statute. The definition of Statute is; “An act of a legislature that declares, proscribes, or commands something; a specific law, expressed in writing. A statute is a written law passed by a legislature on the state or federal level. Statutes set forth general propositions of law that courts apply to specific situations." Legal Dictionary
I understand The Ministerial Instructions to be “instructions” supplementing Canadian Immigration law under IRPA and IRPR. As per the following the Minister has the authority under IRPA section
10.3 to provide “instructions" for the implementation of IRPA and IRPR as follows; “The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, pursuant to section 10.3 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, gives the annexed “Ministerial Instructions" Respecting Invitations to Apply for Permanent Residence under the Express Entry System (March 1, 2017)."
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
As you have stated the Express Entry profile is not an application but rather a process to file an application. You are correct that there is no provision to file an application under substituted evaluation in Express Entry but in my opinion this is legally incorrect because;
My understanding is that the Ministerial Instructions do not have authority to overrule legal statutes defined in IRPA and IRPR
Express Entry as described in the “Ministerial Instructions” is a process and it does not usurp the legal statute under IRPR 76(3) which grants a foreign national (FN) an option to submit an application for permanent residence (PR) to Canada if the FN cannot meet the point requirement under the FSWC but can prove that they can become economically established in Canada
Therefore in my opinion the “Express Entry process” must provide an option to file an application for PR to Canada under IRPR 76(3). In my opinion the Express Entry process has an obligation to provide all options to file a PR application as defined in IRPA and IRPR.
In view of my email reply, please kindly address the following;
How and when will IRCC revise Express Entry to allow a FN to submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation?
How can a FN submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation, until an actual revision is made to Express Entry?
Thank you and I await your reply.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
REP-2017-0499
Dear
We have consulted on your questions with our legal and policy experts. Thank you for your patience.
Your questions are highlighted with our responses below.
1) My understanding is that the Ministerial Instructions do not have authority to overrule legal statutes defined in IRPA and IRPR. The Minister has the authority to give expression of interest instructions that are more stringent than the Act or the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (the Regulations). Subsection 10.3(5) of the Act clarifies that instructions governing any matters related to the expression of interest scheme may provide for criteria that are more stringent than the criteria or requirements provided for in or under any other Division of the Act regarding applications for permanent residence.
2) Express Entry as described in the “Ministerial Instructions" is a process and it does not usurp the legal statute under IRPR 76(3) which grants a foreign national (FN) an option to submit an application for permanent residence (PR) to Canada if the FN cannot meet the point requirement under the FSWC but can prove that they can become economically established in Canada.
3) Therefore in my opinion the “Express Entry process” must provide an option to file an application for PR to Canada under IRPR 76(3). In my opinion the Express Entry process has an obligation to provide all options to file a PR application as defined in IRPA and IRPR. An expression of interest is not an application for permanent residence. A foreign national submitting an expression of interest through the Express Entry system is not an applicant for permanent residence. Rather, the purpose of the expression of interest is to allow IRCC to determine whether the candidate may be eligible to apply as a permanent residence. In their expression of interest, the candidate is not asked to provide documentation proving their eligibility, nor are they asked to pay any processing fees.
4) How and when will IRCC revise Express Entry to allow a FN to submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation? How can a FN submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation, until an actual revision is made to Express Entry? To be eligible to be invited to make an application as a member of a class subject to the expression of interest, a foreign national must meet the eligibility criteria that are set out at section 5 of the Ministerial Instructions for the Express Entry Application Management System. The eligibility criteria include meeting the requirements of the Federal Skilled Worker, Federal Skilled Trades, or Canadian Experience Class if the expression of interest were to be considered an application for a permanent resident visa.
Citoyenneté Canada
Substituted evaluation by officers cannot be used to determine whether the foreign national meets the eligibility criteria. Subsection 10.3(3) of the Act provides that the Minister is to use an electronic system to, among other things, carry out any applicable instructions governing any matters related to the expression of interest scheme and to determine whether the foreign national is eligible to be invited to make an application.
For greater certainty, subsection 5(2) of the Ministerial Instructions for the Express Entry Application Management System was recently amended, to clarify to officers the fact that they must not substitute their evaluation to the determination of whether or not the foreign national meets the criteria to be eligible to be invited to make an application.
We hope that this information will be helpful to you.
Sincerely, Immigration Representative Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
This is in response to your inquiry regarding Restoration. As per program guidelines, if the foreign national has lost their temporary resident status and submits their application within 90 days of losing their status, they may not continue to work or attend school. However, the foreign national must continue to meet the requirements of their stay and meet all the conditions of their permit. In order to apply for restoration, the applicant must continue to meet all eligibility criteria for an extension of their permit. For example, applicants seeking a study permit extension, they must provide proof of acceptance or enrolment in a designated learning institution. threads.question:
TFW holds a work permit that names an employer in Canada; it was issued under the AlESEC (Association for the International Exchange of Students in Economics and Commerce).
I assume that full time work experience gained in Canada under an employer-specific AlESEC work permit for a NOC A position counts as work experience for both CEC and FSW (to get to one year of continuous full time employment)?
However, can you confirm with specific reference to AlESEC?
The holder has graduated e.g. they have completed their degree if that matters.
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good day,
Based on the information that you provided, we understand that the candidate:
1. Completed their studies prior to coming to Canada to work under the AlESEC program.
2. Works in Canada under an employer-specific work permit, and has done so for at least one year.
3. This position is in a NOC A occupation.
4. The candidate is paid by the employer for the work that they have completed (ie. They are not receiving a stipend)
Based on the information that you have provided, it appears that the candidate would meet the following requirements for Canadian work experience to claim Comprehensive Ranking System Points and meet the qualifications of the Canadian Experience Class:
In order for work experience to be considered Canadian for the purpose of the Canadian Experience Class, a candidates skilled work experience must:
be in a job classified as skill type 0, or skill level A or B according to the 2011 National Occupational Classification, amount to at least one year of full-time (or an equal amount in part-time) in the previous three years, have been acquired with an employer in Canada (self-employment does not count), be an activity for which wages were paid or a commission was earned; be gained with the proper legal authorization (for example, as a documented worker with a valid work permit), and not be gained while studying on a student permit.
Please note that any period of employment during which time the foreign national was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating work experience under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), nor will it count for the purposes of points assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). This includes any Canadian work experience that is gained while a student is on an academic break or a co-op term. If the candidate was engaged in full time study at the time of their work experience, they may be able to claim their work experience under the Federal Skilled Worker Program.
If the candidate has an offer of full-time employment from the employer that is on their work permit, they may be able to receive points for a valid job offer in the Comprehensive Ranking System. See the following link for more information: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/exempt.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/exempt.asp)

Hello
This is in response to your enquiry from August 10th regarding post graduate work permit program (PGWpp) eligibility and regularly scheduled breaks. Please see below answers to each of your question: Question 1: Are students eligible for a PGwP if they took a scheduled break, as defined in the section of the website applicable to off-campus work? Answer: Yes, full time students who took regularly scheduled breaks, as defined in the Off-campus work program delivery instructions, are still eligible to PGWPP. Question 2: If a student's break meets the definition of a scheduled break, but does not fall during a traditional period, such as if a student takes the winter semester off rather than the summer semester, would they be eligible for a PGWP? Answer: Yes, the regularly scheduled break is a break taken between academic sessions (such as winter/summer holidays) as determined by the DLl. Thus, it can be taken in summer or in winter if the DLl recognizes it as a scheduled break. Question 3: Is there a maximum number of scheduled breaks that may be taken during the course of the year in order for a student to still be considered eligible for a PGwP? Answer: The regularly scheduled breaks' schedule is determined by each DLI. Therefore, IRCC does not define a maximum number of scheduled breaks that may be taken during the course of the year. For PGWPP eligibility purposes, the student must hold a full-time status during the academic session prior to, as well as subsequent to their institution's scheduled break. threads.subject: Question re: change in US position impacting Canadian work permit-REP-2017-0461
threads.question:
Hello,
and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
Thank you for your email. I would like a response as to the appropriate action for an employer and employee to take in this situation, if possible. Thank you!
Best,
threads.answer:
Hello
Thank you for your continued patience, it is much appreciated.
Please find below the response to your query.
Question
We have a client who has an employee that came to Canada as an Intra-Company Transferee. In that application, we confirmed that the foreign national would remain an employee of the US company, would remain on the US payroll, and would only travel to Canada intermittently as required to fulfill the conditions of his role. He is having a role change in the US that will no longer require him to come to Canada to work, though he will come periodically to attend meetings. It is a voluntary role reduction, and his salary, etc will be less. However, he will only enter Canada now to attend meetings.
There is no formal method for cancelling a work permit, so we ask if there is any proactive (steps) an employer should make in this situation, or is it something that if/when audited, it is addressed?
Answer
If the foreign national will no longer be an intra-company transferee-which is a job covered under the International Mobility Program that is exempt from the requirement for the employer to obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) - and the job duties are changing and the salary is changing/decreasing, the foreign national may need to apply for a new work permit in order to be authorized to come to Canada. (There is no way to cancel an existing work permit; a new work permit can still be obtained, if necessary.) The employer will need to re-assess whether the new job duties in Canada requires a work permit or not, and if so, whether it requires an LMlA or is LMIA-exempt (which means the employer would need to submit a new Offer of Employment in the Employer Portal).
Authorization to work temporarily in Canada is given [IRPR 200.(1)(c)(ii.1)] based on the work permit application which stated the job the foreign national would be doing (National Occupation Code NOC), the employer, and the work location. A foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. Providing a salary that is different, i.e. lower, than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC, after the work permit was issued would require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit and the employer to submit a new Offer of Employment (if the job has changed and the new job requires a work permit and an Offer of Employment).
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations [183(1)(b) and 185].
As per 209.2(1) of the IRPR, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
and Citizenship Caneda
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province
in which the foreign national works;
provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
To clarify, in cases where the job has changed, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. A new work permit may be required, and the foreign national will not be authorized to work in Canada in the new duties until a new work permit is obtained. Furthermore, if a random inspection is initiated for the first offer of employment, the inspection will still assess compliance for the entire period of the former work permit. If the employer was inconsistent in providing the foreign worker exactly what was stated in the Offer of Employment, then the employer will have to justify those differences with documentation i.e. how, why and when the job changed, and that a new work permit was obtained for the new job.
If a new work permit for the change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non- compliance by the employer.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.
We hope that this information is helpful to you and once again please accept our apologies for the delay in responding to your query.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

RE: Apply for citizenship under Humanitarian and Compassionate grounds-REP-2017-1829
Thank you for your question.
Within the citizenship context, there is no specific avenue for humanitarian and compassionate exemption of the physical presence requirement. By way of subsection 5(4) of the Citizenship Act, the Minister may at his discretion, grant citizenship to alleviate cases of statelessness, or of special and unusual hardship or to reward services of an exceptional value to Canada. Therefore, if your client believes he is deserving of a discretionary grant of citizenship on the basis of special and unusual hardship or exceptional services to Canada, he can make an application under subsection 5(1) requesting discretionary consideration under 5(4) and provide documentation to support the request. When posted, this updated procedure will specify that requests to withdraw a citizenship application my be held in abeyance if:

This is to prevent applicants from circumventing the penalty of a five year prohibition on citizenship eligibility as a result of misrepresentation (paragraph 22(1)(e.2)). threads.answer:
#### Thank you for your enquiry.
The forms IMM 1344, IMM 0008 and IMM 5533, have been updated to reflect the regulatory change for dependent children. The changes to these forms do not affect an applicant unless they may have a dependent child who would fall under the new definition implemented on October 24, 2017.
For more information, please visit these web sites:
News release: New definition of age of dependants now in force [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/2017/10/new](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/2017/10/new) definition ofageofdependantsnowinforce.html
Backgrounder: Determining who is eligible as a dependant [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/2017/10/determining](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/news/2017/10/determining) who iseligibleasadependantunderthepublicpolicyonthea.html
The best way to ensure that you are providing the most accurate possible information is to use the most updated version of the form.
However, we will accept the previous version of these forms in this case IF the applicant does not have a dependent child who would fall under the new definition, AND provides a written statement confirming that he/she is not affected by the regulatory change for dependent children (meaning that he/she does not have a dependent child aged 19, 20, or 21 who would not have qualified for inclusion prior to October 24, 2017). You can attach a copy of this message to the application package.
Thank you,

What is a peer review? A peer review is an independent assessment of a commitment by a panel of experts convened by the industry association that represents the lead designated entity on the Commitment Certificate. For example, if the Commitment Certificate was issued by a designated angel investor group. then the National Angel Capital Organization is responsible for organizing a peer review panel to evaluate the commitment. The peer review process was designed to build in safeguards to protect against fraud and to ensure that the deals made between private-sector partners and foreign entrepreneurs are in accordance with industry standards.
When must a peer review be done?
The peer review process must be initiated:
when the visa officer has concerns about the Commitment Certificate and/or whether the designated entity has performed due diligence according to industry standards; and for quality assurance on a random basis.

All peer reviews are initiated by a visa officer at (IRCC). The visa officer will complete the Peer Review Request form (IMM 5765) and send it to the industry association naned in the application. The industry association must then assemble a panel of experts within four weeks.

Dear Ms.
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We trust that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question #1:
I note that the attached indicates in multiple places that the business incubator must confirm that it has performed due diligence on various requirements including control over any intellectual property or other assets that they are bringing to the business, the applicant, business and investment. What exactly would be required of the business in this regard?
Response #1:
Applicants (Businesses) must meet the following requirements to be found eligible under the Start-up Visa program:
have a Letter of Support from a designated angel investor group, venture capital fund or business incubator meet the ownership requirements for a qualifying business get scores of at least Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 5 in all four categories for either English or French, and have an adequate amount of money to settle and provide for the cost of living prior to earning an income.
Designated entities are required to perform a due diligence assessment of the applicants and the applicants' business in accordance with industry standards. IRCC provides business incubators essential information that should be included on the term sheet/client agreement and the commitment certificate. This will assist officers in assessing whether or not sufficient due diligence has been performed on an application under the Start-up visa program. However, IRCC looks to the industry associations to advise on what is standard for the industry and whether those standards have been met. In cases where the visa officers have questions about the due diligence performed by a designated entity, or on a random basis (for quality assurance), the visa officers may send the case to the industry association to conduct a peer review. A peer review is an independent assessment of a commitment by a panel of experts convened by the industry
association that represents the lead designated entity on the Commitment Certificate. The peer review
process was designed to build in safeguards to protect against fraud and to ensure that the deals made between private sector partners and foreign entrepreneurs are in accordance with industry standards. Section 11 of the Ministerial Instructions outline the grounds for review and the need for an independent assessment or peer review.
Question # 2:
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
What is the risk to a business incubator with respect to the commitments that it is making to supporting a new start up business under this program if for example the due diligence was found inadequate and the application was
unsuccessful? Is there a guide for Business Incubators to refer to?
Response# 2:
- If, at the end of their determination, the visa officers are not satisfied that the designated entity performed sufficient due diligence, the applicants' permanent resident applications can be refused. This is stated under section 9 of the Ministerial Instructions: 9(2) If the officer is not satisfied that the entity assessed the applicant and the applicant's business in a manner consistent with industry standards or that the terms of the commitment are consistent with industry standards, the officer may refuse to issue the permanent resident visa. We hope this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Work Permit validity when company purchased by another-REP-2017-1823
threads.question:
Good afternoon;
My client is working for company x in Canada. Company x is in the process of being sold to company y. This is an asset sale. On purchase the company will continue to operate under the same operating name, the nature of the business and the location will remain the same and the employee will continue to work in the same position. The only thing that will change tis that the legal ownership of the company will transfer from one numbered company to another.
My understanding in this type of case is that no new work permit is required, given the fact that the employee will be working for the same operation named in his work permit, in the same position, in the same location, etc.
Will you kindly advise as to what is required in these circumstances.
中 and Citizenship Caneda
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your questions. Updated guidance regarding mergers and acquisitions will be available online shortly.
The main consideration for temporary workers who hold employer-specific work permits is whether the new organization can be seen to be a “successor in interest" employer, or, in the case of an acquisition, the same employer. Changes in ownership structure should not require a new LMiA or Offer of employment if the new organization assumes the previous owner's assets and liabilities (including those of the prior owner relating to the hiring and retention of temporary workers
e.g. where a “successor in interest" can be demonstrated). To establish a “successor in interest", the successor entity must demonstrate – in the event of an employer compliance inspection-that it has substantially assumed the interests and obligations, assets and liabilities of the original owner, and continues to operate the same type of business as the original owner. If the take-over organization is a “successor in interest" in that it has substantially assumed the interests and obligations, assets and liabilities of the original organization (wholly or partially), and continues to operate the same type of business as the original organization, then the take-over organization would remain the ‘employer' for the purpose of the existing work permit as well. The temporary worker is not obligated to obtain a new work permit, and will continue to be authorized to work in Canada for the duration of the period stated on the existing work permit, if: ●
the take-over organization meets the requirements that the LMIA-exempt work permit was issued under (e.g.,
qualifying relationship for intra-company transferee) or the take-over organization assumes the LMiA contract,
and
- the worker's employment conditions as per the original offer of employment, for example, the wage, duties, location, have not changed
If the take-over organization does not become a “successor in interest", that is, it does not assume all of the interests/obligations, assets/liabilities of the original organization, then a new LMiA or Offer of employment and new work permits are required for all temporary workers holding employer-specific work permits, and the employee should cease working for the take-over organization until a new work permit have been obtained. The new organization is responsible for ensuring that it only employs a foreign national in a capacity in which the foreign national is authorized under the IRPA to be employed, as per A124(1)(c).
Employers are advised to retain all documentation related to a merger or acquisition for six years. An inspection may be initiated from the first day of employment for which a work permit is issued up to a maximum of six years thereafter.
We hope this information is helpful.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Work permit holder no longer working for company-REP-2017-2110
threads.question:
Dear Sirs/Mesdames:
A Canadian company had an onsite inspection today by Integrity Services Branch, ESDC, for a specific LMIA. The person specified on the LMIA by the Canadian company has quit the job.
According to the Integrity Services Branch officer, the Canadian company is required to inform ESDC which was done AND IRCC that the foreign national no longer works for their company as of the last day the foreign national worked.
We need your directions on which IRCC office should be sent this information and its contact information, email address, fax number or office address if it is required to be posted to this specific IRCC office.
Thank you.
Regards,
Citoyenneté Canada
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Question:
re informing IRCC that the foreign national no longer works for their company as of the last day the foreign national worked. We need your directions on which IRCC office should be sent this information and its contact information, email address, fax number or office address if it is required to be posted to this specific IRCC office.
Answer:
There is no need to inform IRCC when a foreign worker leaves employment.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the
province in which the foreign national works;
provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit (nor is a new Offer of Employment required to be submitted) unless there has been a change in employer, occupation or location.
After a work permit has been issued to the foreign worker, IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes that are part of the regulatory imposed conditions on the employer, such as wages, working conditions, location, etc.
However, the regulations state that the employer must keep all documents pertaining to the employment of the foreign national for six years beginning on the first day of employment, including any documentation supporting the termination of employment. If there are any changes to the information that differs from what was provided in the Offer of Employment, then the employer will (if asked during a compliance inspection) have to provide the documentation that justified the change as per subsection R203(1.1).
The Voluntary Disclosure mechanism was put in place to allow employers who found themselves to be non-compliant with the conditions outlined under R203(1) to inform IRCC. Disclosure of a termination of employment would not be necessary unless the relevant provincial/territorial guidelines were not followed.
More information is available on our website at the following link:

threads.answer:
Good morning,
Thank you for your inquiry. Please find the response to your questions below:
- Are applicants who have engaged in 24 months of full-time work in Canada and part-time studies in Canada on a study permit eligible? The applicant must demonstrate that they have obtained a total of at least 24 months of authorized full-time work experience in Canada within the 48 months before their complete application is received. Full-time work means at least 30 hours of paid work per week. Any periods of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included when calculating the period of qualifying work experience. There is nothing to restrict an applicant from using work experience that was acquired while they were engaged in part-time studies on a valid study permit. It would be on the applicant to satisfy the officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies at the time the work experience was acquired. Are applicants who have engaged in 24 months of full-time work in Canada and full-time studies outside of Canada via distance learning eligible? Any periods of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included when calculating the period of qualifying work experience. This includes full-time studies outside of Canada via distance learning. Are the criteria used to assess whether an institution/program will be found eligible for an ECA publicly available? No, ECA organizations do not make this information publically available, but all of IRCC's seven designated ECA organizations require the credentials to be from institutions recognized by the source country as part of their own procedures and quality control. This effectively parallels the requirements of Canadian learning institutions, as set out in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). We encourage clients to contact the ECA organizations directly to learn more about their policies and procedures.
I trust this information will assist you.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Travailleur, statut implicite et NAS expiré-REP-2017-2129
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Un détenteur de PVT actuellement à l’emploi dont une demande de parrainage entre conjoints a été soumise de l’intérieur du Canada avant expiration du PVT (avec demande de permis de travail ouvert tel que le permet le projet pilote actuellement en vigueur) sera considéré, à l’expiration de son PVT, comme étant en statut implicite jusqu’à décision sur sa demande de permis de travail ouvert.
Dans un tel cas, cette personne est-elle autorisée à travailler considérant que son NAS a expiré en même temps que son PVT ? Si oui, à quelles conditions?
La situation est-elle différente si le travailleur souhaite être embauché par un nouvel employeur pendant qu’il est en statut implicite?
Merci par avance.
Cordialement
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Bonjour-Pour faire suite à la question ci-dessous et compte tenu des renseignements présentés, la personne pourrait être
autorisée de continuer à travailler sous les même conditions de son permis de travail Vacances Travail du
programme Expérience Internationale Canada jusqu’à ce qu’une décision soit prise sur sa nouvelle demande de
permis de travail ouvert sous la catégorie des époux ou conjoints de fait au Canada (ECFC). Il faut noter que le permis de travail sous la catégorie Vacance Travail est un permis de travail ouvert. Dans le cadre du Programme de mobilité internationale, le permis de travail ouvert permet à une personne de travailler pour n’importe quel employeur pendant une période déterminée.
Un résident temporaire doit présenter une demande pour prolonger sa période de séjour autorisé avant qu’elle ne prenne fin. Si cela a été fait, la période de séjour autorisé à titre de résident temporaire est prolongée en vertu de la loi jusqu’à ce qu’une décision soit prise [R183(5)]. Il est considéré qu’une telle personne a un statut implicite de résident temporaire au cours de cette période.
Si un résident temporaire demande le renouvellement de son permis de travail et que son permis expire avant qu’une décision ne soit prise, l’alinéa 186u) du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR) (le droit de continuer à travailler selon les conditions imposées jusqu’à ce qu’une décision soit prise au sujet de la demande de renouvellement) s’appliquent tant et aussi longtemps que la personne demeure au Canada.
Pour ce qui est de l'information sur le NAS, veuillez consulter le site internet du ministère d' Emploi et
Développement social Canada pour de plus amples renseignements.
Merci, Passe une belle journée,

The instructions for assessing an electronic application on section A11.2 stating “A11.2 does not apply when an applicant adds a family member to their application after the e-APR" are intended for situations in which there are changes to the applicant's family during the application process (e.g: birth, marriage).
In any situation where the spouse changes from non-accompanying to accompanying in an Express Entry application, the eligibility of the principal applicant may be re-assesed at any time until permanent residence is granted. The application can be refused if the recalculated CRS score is lower than the minimum score of the round in which they were invited. However, in an Express Entry application where the spouse is not going be processed and will not receive a visa at the time of finalization, where the intention of the Principal Applicant is to become a permanent resident of Canada as a single person and then perhaps use the sponsorship process later, then, subject to all other requirements of the sponsorship process, the permanent resident would be eligible to sponsor the spouse.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The offer of employment number has no strict expiry date, however it is important that the information (including start date and duration of work) contained in the offer of employment accurately reflects the work the foreign national will do.
IRCC understands that the foreign national or the employer may not have control over when the foreign national can actually travel. The start date is a best estimate. If the foreign national is unable to arrive in Canada until well beyond the expected start date, we recommend that the offer be withdrawn and a new one submitted with more accurate information.

The following cases provide guidance as to when foreign nationals can benefit from short-term work permit exemptions if they have already used another short-term exemption: If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may they be granted from the same exemption again?
